title: The Multilingual Frontier for Insects as Food and Feed
content: Effective science communication and knowledge transfer rely on accessible data dissemination. While academic research is predominantly published in English, critical information pertaining to farmed insect diversity, life-history traits, and rearing practices often remain trapped in non-English publications, theses, and grey literature. Conversely, the availability of a research publication in English does not automatically entail its usability for local stakeholders; rather, scientific findings frequently fail to reach the farmers, breeders, officials, regulators, and policy makers who need them most. As such, communicating science across languages requires a reciprocal and bidirectional exchange of information that integrates local insights into the global evidence base, and also translates advances published in English back into regional languages. Disruptions from either side of this process can entrench knowledge shortfalls and lead to inefficient use of resources that might duplicate work that has already been achieved previously or elsewhere. Moreover, effective multilingual science communication is especially vital for the global field of Insects as Food and Feed (IFF), which relies heavily on collaborations between the Global North and Global South. To address this complex issue, we outline methods within insect science to promote multilingual publishing efforts, which act as a vital pillar of open and FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable) publishing principles. Lastly, even with the proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) and large language model (LLM) use in science, we maintain that multilingual publishing will be critical now and in the future for society to effectively respond to global crises in agriculture, public health, and biodiversity.
